Q: GCC vs Clang when packing array<uint8_t,N> into uint64_t A:

The disassembly output of clang is missleading.

All what the pack and hash functions do in the shown disassembly is to return a logical AND on the argument address, which appears rather to look like a place holder rather than actual code. If you try to give the compiler something it cannot infer anything on, e.g.

int main() {
    I a,b,c,d,e,f;
    std::cin >> a >> b >> c >> d >> e >> f;
    key_type aa{ a,b,c,d,e,f };
    std::cout << cast_and_shift::hash(aa);
}

what you get for the disassembly is:

main:
        push    rax
        mov     rdi, qword ptr [rip + std::cin@GOTPCREL]
        lea     rsi, [rsp + 6]
        call    std::basic_istream<char, std::char_traits<char>>& std::operator>><char, std::char_traits<char>>(std::basic_istream<char, std::char_traits<char>>&, char&)@PLT
        lea     rsi, [rsp + 5]
        mov     rdi, rax
        [...]
        call    std::basic_istream<char, std::char_traits<char>>& std::operator>><char, std::char_traits<char>>(std::basic_istream<char, std::char_traits<char>>&, char&)@PLT
        movzx   eax, byte ptr [rsp + 6]
        movzx   esi, byte ptr [rsp + 5]
        movzx   ecx, byte ptr [rsp + 4]
        movzx   edx, byte ptr [rsp + 2]
        movzx   edi, byte ptr [rsp + 1]
        shl     rdi, 40
        shl     rdx, 32
        movzx   r8d, byte ptr [rsp + 3]
        shl     r8d, 24
        shl     ecx, 16
        shl     esi, 8
        or      rsi, rax
        or      rsi, rcx
        or      rsi, r8
        or      rsi, rdx
        or      rsi, rdi
        mov     rdi, qword ptr [rip + std::cout@GOTPCREL]
        call    std::ostream& std::ostream::_M_insert<unsigned long>(unsigned long)@PLT
        xor     eax, eax
        pop     rcx
        ret

for clang and

main:
        sub     rsp, 24
        mov     edi, OFFSET FLAT:std::cin
        lea     rsi, [rsp+9]
        call    std::basic_istream<char, std::char_traits<char>>& std::operator>><char, std::char_traits<char>>(std::basic_istream<char, std::char_traits<char>>&, char&)
        [...]
        call    std::basic_istream<char, std::char_traits<char>>& std::operator>><char, std::char_traits<char>>(std::basic_istream<char, std::char_traits<char>>&, char&)
        movzx   esi, BYTE PTR [rsp+10]
        movzx   eax, BYTE PTR [rsp+11]
        mov     edi, OFFSET FLAT:std::cout
        sal     rax, 16
        sal     rsi, 8
        or      rsi, rax
        movzx   eax, BYTE PTR [rsp+9]
        or      rsi, rax
        movzx   eax, BYTE PTR [rsp+12]
        sal     rax, 24
        or      rsi, rax
        movzx   eax, BYTE PTR [rsp+13]
        sal     rax, 32
        or      rsi, rax
        movzx   eax, BYTE PTR [rsp+14]
        sal     rax, 40
        or      rsi, rax
        call    std::ostream& std::ostream::_M_insert<unsigned long>(unsigned long)
        xor     eax, eax
        add     rsp, 24
        ret

for gcc (similar for the mem_cpy version). Apart from inlining the functions (including the actual hashing algorithm) alltogether, both compilers seem to deliver equivalently quick code: https://godbolt.org/z/b9MoMeTv1

Q: Make UserString behave like str A:

I think this is best answered by this: https://stackoverflow.com/a/59882723/9628272

The UserString isn't a str, so there isn't (AFAIK) a "clean" or non-hacked way to make it look like a string right now. I don't think you can trust every library (or even most) to duck-type strings. Therefore, when it comes to:

  • The default file writer does an isinstance(...,str) call before writing a sting

  • json.dumps does not accept UserString as keys (even though they are just str)

I think the best thing to do is to just call str() or .data on the object. You're already serializing (one way or another) so the "lazy" value of the object will already be consumed at this point.

As for:

  • pydantic is very ... pedantic on types it warns on UserString where str is expected but also fails on serialisation and model dumping

I believe pydantic allows you to customize serialization with decorated methods, see docs here

Not related to answer: the way your example class is set up, each time .data is called the function is re-run. Unless the function can change at run time, it's worth considering storing result after it's been run once so it never needs to run again. This could just be due to the simplified example, but I assume you wouldn't be using lazy strings unless our_func had some tangible performance cost. Obviously not applicable if memory is the reason you're evaluating lazily instead of performance.

Q: Using LLM models downloaded from huggingface with langgraph A:

You can use the huggingface models lovally via the ChatHuggingface integration wrapper. At first you need to install an additional package into your environment:

pip install langchain-huggingface

and afterwards you can initialise it with the follwing code:

import torch
from langchain_huggingface import ChatHuggingFace, HuggingFacePipeline

model_id = ''

llm = HuggingFacePipeline.from_model_id(
    model_id=model_id,
    task="text-generation",
    model_kwargs={"dtype": torch.bfloat16, "device_map":"auto",},
)

chat_model = ChatHuggingFace(llm=llm)

This replace the init_chat_model in your example and the next step is to bind the model:

# Define tools
@tool
def multiply(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    ...

@tool
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    ...

@tool
def divide(a: int, b: int) -> float:
    ...


# Augment the LLM with tools
tools = [add, multiply, divide]
tools_by_name = {tool.name: tool for tool in tools}
model_with_tools = model.bind_tools(tools)

Q: How can I use async/await at the top level? A:

2023 answer: you can now use top level await in all supported versions of node.js

Most of the answers above are a little out of date, comtain unrelated info (no, using .then() is not top level wait) or are very verbose, so here's a quick example for current node.

In JavaScript (not using TypeScript) using a .js file and type: module

Make a file called runme.js:

import { exec as oldExec } from "node:child_process";
import { promisify } from "node:util";
const exec = promisify(oldExec);
const log = console.log.bind(console);

// Top level await works now
const { stdout, stderr } = await exec("ls -la");
log("Output:\n", stdout);
log("\n\nErrors:\n", stderr);

Then set type: module in package.json. Run node runme.js

Output:

drwxr-xr-x 30 mike mike 4096 Aug 12 11:05 ..
-rw-r--r--  1 mike mike  130 Aug 12 12:01 file.json
-rw-r--r--  1 mike mike  770 Aug 12 12:12 runme.mjs

Run node runme.mjs

Output:

Errors:

You don't need to set type: module in your package.json because .mjs files are assumed to be ESM.

In TypeScript using tsx

Yes, tsx has nothing to do the 'tsx' from react.js. It's a tool that executes TypeScript.

In TypeScript, using tsx.

  • Edit your package.json to add
  "type": "module",

Run

npm i tsx

Then run:

npx tsx runme.ts

Which will return:
